summary: Pupils aged 9–11 learn to classify symbiosis — close, long-term relationships between different species — by reasoning from the outcome for each partner (benefit +, no clear effect 0, or harm –) rather than recalling labels. Mutualism is +/+, commensalism +/0, and parasitism +/–. The core skill is classifying a NEW pair by asking 'what does each side gain or lose?', while distinguishing symbiosis from a quick predatory kill or from competition within a species.
misconceptions: 'Symbiosis always means both animals help each other' — mutualism does, but parasitism harms one partner and commensalism helps only one.
'A predator eating prey is symbiosis' — predation is a brief lethal act, not a close ongoing relationship.
'Parasites want to kill their host' — most parasites keep the host alive; a dead host is a lost home/food supply.
'Commensalism means no effect at all ever' — the second partner is not clearly benefited or harmed, but effects can be subtle/hard to measure.
'Only animals form symbioses' — many involve plants, fungi, and microbes (bee–flower, coral–algae, gut bacteria).

activities.title: Classify the relationship from outcomes
steps: For each presented pair — clownfish and anemone, remora and shark, tick and deer, a bird nesting in a tree — mark the outcome for EACH partner as benefit (+), no clear effect (0), or harm (–).
Read off the resulting type from the two marks: +/+ = mutualism, +/0 = commensalism, +/– = parasitism.
Meet a brand-new pair (e.g. barnacles on a whale) you were not taught and classify it yourself by asking 'does the whale lose anything?'
When a card shows predation (a lion eating a zebra) or competition between members of the same species, reject it as NOT symbiosis and say why.
On deliberately fuzzy cases, choose a 'not enough evidence' response if the second partner's gain or loss is genuinely hard to tell.
activities.insight: The three vocabulary words become a reusable reasoning tool: any close, ongoing relationship between different species can be classified by tracking each partner's cost or benefit, so a harmful case (parasitism) still counts as symbiosis.

activities.title: Gallery of paired organisms (scaffold)
steps: Explore illustrated species pairs — clownfish–anemone, remora–shark, tick–deer, barnacle–whale — including symbioses with a non-animal partner: bee–flower, coral–algae, and gut bacteria in an animal's gut.
Reveal each partner's gain or loss — e.g. tapping a partner to show what it gains or loses — and note the resulting type.
After exploring, predict the type for the NEXT pair before revealing the outcomes.
activities.insight: Concrete canonical examples build a stock of cases and show that symbioses can involve non-animal partners too — a plant (bee–flower), algae (coral–algae) and microbes (gut bacteria) — not only animals.

activities.title: Sort and classify check
steps: Sort a set of pairs into mutualism, commensalism and parasitism.
Answer a multiple-choice item classifying a new scenario and justify the choice.
Reject distractor cards showing predation or same-species competition as not-symbiosis.
activities.insight: Confirms the learner can distinguish the three types and holds the boundary that predation and competition are not symbiosis.

activities.title: Marine-biologist-in-role: is this really commensalism? (optional hook)
steps: In a short role-play discussion, argue whether a given relationship (e.g. barnacles on a whale) is truly commensalism.
Raise ways the 'unaffected' partner might actually be slightly helped or harmed, and what evidence would settle it.
activities.insight: Clean categories are a scientific simplification — commensalism is genuinely hard to verify, and good classification admits uncertainty.

checkQuestion: A tick lives on a deer, drinking its blood and giving nothing back. Some people say symbiosis only means animals helping each other, so this can't be symbiosis. Are they right? Is the tick-and-deer relationship symbiosis — and if so, what kind?
checkAnswer: They are wrong. Symbiosis means any close, long-term relationship between two different species, and it comes in kinds depending on who benefits: mutualism (both gain, like clownfish and anemone), commensalism (one gains and the other is unaffected, like a remora riding a shark), and parasitism (one gains at the other's expense, like the tick harming the deer). The tick-and-deer relationship is parasitism — which is a type of symbiosis — so symbiosis is not only about helping.
